title: Kula Disaster Recovery Update Meeting: January 31, 2024

issues.title: Kula burn scar fencing and native replanting

recap.headline: Kula fire recovery: debris removal done, survey results shared, insurance questions
recap.in_60_seconds: Maui County, state and federal agencies held a Kula disaster recovery update at the invitation of the area's Councilmember. The new Maui Emergency Management administrator introduced himself, the Department of Health reported no asbestos in the latest air samples, and the Department of Water said fire-related water advisories are lifted and long-term monitoring continues. The Councilmember announced that debris removal in Kula is 100% done, and staff shared 17 needs survey responses sorted into six recovery areas. Three residents spoke, raising how leftover insurance debris coverage will be collected, debris outside the cleared areas, wind damage, trees over power lines, road damage and a green waste site. Many of the last resident's questions were put on the record without answers.

parts.title: Welcome and agenda
presented: Mayor thanked the Councilmember who asked for the meeting and the state Department of Health staff who flew in from Oʻahu.
The agenda covered updates from emergency management and the Department of Health, needs survey results and next steps.
The Army Corps of Engineers wrapped up its Kula work the week before.

parts.title: New Maui Emergency Management administrator
presented: The new administrator is a retired Maui Fire Department battalion chief with 25 years of service.
He is working on resiliency through education, preparedness, hazard mitigation, infrastructure and response.

next.what: Meeting with the Councilmember and community at Pukalani Community Center to discuss concerns in more detail

parts.title: Department of Health and Department of Water updates
parts.presenter: Department of Health deputy director for environmental health; Department of Water Supply deputy director
presented: Purple air sensors stay in Kula for now; some E-BAM monitors were moved to Lahaina for debris removal there.
The latest air sample results, posted online last week, showed no asbestos and very low heavy metal detections.
The last unsafe water advisory was lifted in October 2023; testing continues for three months per area, then quarterly for one to two years.
Reservoirs are 85% full; the Waiakoa farm lot tank is offline because it leaks and is scheduled to be replaced.

next.what: Clear the rest of the Waiakoa farm lot tank property

parts.title: Needs assessment survey results
parts.presenter: County communications director; Office of Recovery contractor staff
presented: 17 people answered the survey: 60% directly impacted, 22% Kula residents, 19% other.
Top themes included rebuilding, watershed and forest recovery, expedited permitting, insurance and hardening utilities.
Input fits the Office of Recovery's six focus areas, including housing, infrastructure, health and social services, natural and cultural resources, economic recovery and community planning.
Residents asked for water testing down to Māʻalaea and Kīhei, erosion control, invasive species control, business grants and answers on whether ash affected nearby farm produce.

next.what: Develop projects and give updates, and seek answers on farm produce impacts

parts.title: Councilmember on next steps
presented: Debris removal in Kula is 100% done.
The next stage is resiliency work, with hope for FEMA grants and support for the watershed alliance.
She wants to keep holding these meetings and bring a session for people with building permits once permitting is worked out through the Council.

next.what: More community meetings, including one on building permits

parts.title: Kula Community Watershed Alliance
presented: The alliance was founded by Kula fire survivors and is led by a survivor neighborhood council.
It began soil stabilization on its eighth acre, filling gaps not covered by the federal NRCS Emergency Watershed Protection Program, which is expected to start in February.
About nine grant proposals are pending; the alliance is written into the Māʻalaea Bay Watershed Management Plan, opening Clean Water Act funding.
The Waiakoa watershed drains to Keālia Pond National Wildlife Refuge, so preventing runoff matters.

next.what: Federal Emergency Watershed Protection work expected to begin

parts.title: Questions on insurance and leftover debris

raised.concern: How the government collects homeowners' insurance debris removal money for the Army Corps cleanup.
Trees and debris left on property because they were not tagged, and whether insurance will cover removing them before money goes back.

answered.said: The Corps and FEMA do not bill residents; the County will review insurance after all Maui debris removal is done, which is a ways off. Opt-in owners should pay zero out of pocket, and money spent on debris removal will not be taken back. Unused money should be held because the County intends to recoup it.
The Army Corps only cleared within its mission boundary. Owners may use their debris coverage to remove items left outside it; any unused amount goes to FEMA, as agreed from the start.

next.what: County review of insurance debris coverage
next.when: after debris removal for all of Maui is complete

parts.title: How the new emergency management administrator was hired
presented: 15 or 16 people applied after the previous administrator resigned.
Emergency managers from four counties narrowed the field to five, who went through an all-day scenario test at UH Maui College.
The administration interviewed the top three; the new administrator had the highest score.

parts.title: More questions and FEMA on mitigation funding

raised.concern: How much wind damage in Kula has been addressed, and whether landowners must report it.
Who cleans debris on vacant lots and outside the ash footprint; Kula is not fully clean.
Making phase two soil sample results available to the whole community.
Trees hanging over and falling on utility lines.
Fixing roads and parking lots damaged by the cleanup.
A green waste facility so people stop dumping in gulches.
Making sure talk leads to action so this never happens again.

answered.said: Wind damage to homes goes through FEMA's individual assistance program; applicants state the cause and an inspector checks it. Owners may get a grant for minimal repairs. He did not have Kula numbers but will look.

FEMA sets aside 15% of disaster spending for mitigation; with about $2.5 billion projected, that is about $375 million for resilience projects at a 75-25 cost share. He urged the community to work with the County and state to set priorities.

next.what: FEMA to look up wind damage figures

parts.title: Closing
presented: Staff thanked the livestream team and said officials would stay afterward to talk.

bills.name: Māʻalaea Bay Watershed Management Plan
bills.what: A watershed plan that now includes the Kula alliance's work, letting it seek Clean Water Act funding.

open_questions.question: Who will clean up fire debris on vacant lots and outside the ash footprint?
How can the community get the phase two soil sample results?
What will be done about trees over utility lines?
Who will fix roads and parking lots damaged by the cleanup?
Will there be a green waste facility for Kula?
Was produce on farms near the fire affected by ash and debris?

not_on_tracker.topic: Insurance debris coverage and debris left outside cleared areas
not_on_tracker.why: Kula owners face costly removal of untagged trees and want to know what insurance money must go back to FEMA.

not_on_tracker.topic: Trees over utility lines in Kula
not_on_tracker.why: A resident saw two trees fall on lines the day of the meeting and fears another fire.
Without one, people dump green waste in gulches.
Roads and parking lots used during cleanup were damaged.

not_on_tracker.topic: Waiakoa farm lot water tank replacement
not_on_tracker.why: The leaking Kula tank is offline and residents asked about overgrowth around it.

moments.quote: Today or actually yesterday, we started soil stabilization on our eighth acre in Kula. And we're just working in places where we understand there won't be government support through the NRCS Emergency Watershed Protection Program.
moments.about: The fire survivor-led watershed group reports it has begun soil stabilization on its eighth acre of the Kula burn area, filling gaps left by federal programs.

moments.quote: So, extremely important that we prevent runoff, sedimentation laws, and all the things. And we're working with Department of Health on the Clean Water Act funding. The Alliance has been written into the Ma'alai'a Bay Watershed Management Plan.
moments.about: The group explains why burn scar stabilization matters for downstream waters and how it is seeking Clean Water Act funding for the work.
